newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech cbank steps up battle with crown speculators.
newsitem.headline: Czech cbank steps up battle with crown speculators.

text.p: The Czech National Bank (CNB) stepped up its battle to support the ailing Czech crown on Thursday, choking market liquidity after speculators pushed the currency to record lows.
CNB board member Ludek Niedermeyer said the central bank, with immediate effect, had agreed with large domestic banks to limit access by non-resident investors to the Czech money market.
He added that the central bank was also immediately closing all access to the Lombard credit facility, used by commercial banks to borrow short-term funds.
"The central bank, after discussions with leading (domestic) banks, has decided steps that would restrain non-residents' access to our money market," Niedermeyer told Reuters.
He said the character of the restriction was temporary and reflected the situation on the foreign exchange market.

"This is not a reaction to events only this morning but to the situation that non-residents are taking big positions on the money market. Basically this is increasing the volatility," Niedermeyer said.

Money market dealers said the moves ground trading to a virtual halt since no funds were available. Market rates on Wednesday sky-rocketed to over 500 percent as banks scrambled to find funds to cover their positions at the end of the minimum reserve period.
The crown, which has been under pressure for over a week, opened steady at about 2.7 percent on the depreciation side of its dollar/mark basket midpoint.

But speculators in London moved in soon afterward, pushing the crown to a record low of -6.4 against basket parity, forcing the central bank to step into the market directly for the third time in a week.
Dealers said the CNB had also been intervening in London by dealing directly with some foreign banks there, and put estimates of the cost of the intervention at some $500 million.
The CNB also raised its one-week repo rate to 75 percent, which, coupled with the moves to limit market liquidity, helped pull the crown back to about -3.00 percent against basket parity.
Dealers warned of the cost of maintaining the crown at current levels, adding they expected the market may try to push the crown out of the band within which the CNB fixes the currency.
"It's (the intervention) unsustainable and...I think that they (speculators) will really now at these levels push it over the band," said Petr Kuklis, a dealer of Girocredit in Prague.

The CNB has been waging a war against investors to keep the crown from crashing since last week when a wave of short-selling pushed the currency to more than five percent below the mid-point of the dollar/mark basket, which the central bank uses to fix the crown's exchange rate daily.
Central bank and government officials to date have adamantly ruled out a devaluation of the currency.
Last Friday the CNB raised the Lombard rate from 14 percent to 50 percent in a move to bolster the crown, once regarded as the most stable currency in post-communist central Europe.
The CNB through the course of the week has gradually restricted access to the Lombard facility, the last resort lending facility for banks, squeezing market liquidity and further boosting the crown.
The central bank fixed the crown at 30.629 to the dollar and 18.081 to the mark on Thursday, implying a deviation against basket parity of -3.00 percent after a fixing of -2.27 percent on Wednesday.
